lead: Fadrozole (brand name Afema, Novartis) is a selective, nonsteroidal, oral aromatase inhibitor that is or has been used in Japan for estrogen-dependent breast cancer [1]. Aromatase is the enzyme that converts androgens into estrogens, so drugs in this class lower estrogen levels; in physique and hormone-optimization circles, aromatase inhibitors are discussed as tools for managing estrogen, including estrogen-related effects such as breast tissue growth (gynecomastia) in men [17][18]. Fadrozole is a second-generation member of the class, classed as Type II (reversible), binding the heme group of the aromatase enzyme [1].

Most published work on fadrozole beyond oncology is laboratory research in which it is used as a tool to block estrogen synthesis in fish, birds and rodents. Human trials from the early 1990s tested it in postmenopausal women with metastatic breast cancer [10][11][12][13]. No published human trial has tested it for appearance outcomes, and it has been largely overtaken by third-generation inhibitors such as anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane [17].

chain: Aromatase inhibitor blocks conversion of androgens to estrogens
Claimed to reduce estrogen-related effects such as breast tissue growth in men
angle.text: Aromatase inhibitors as a class are used in medicine for gynecomastia and in off-label estrogen management during testosterone therapy, and are discussed in physique communities for the same reason [17][18]. Fadrozole itself has been studied in breast cancer and animals, not for appearance.

infobox: About 82% at 1 mg daily; about 93% at 2 mg twice daily in postmenopausal women [1]

paras: Fadrozole has been used for estrogen-dependent breast cancer in Japan [1]. Related drugs in the class are used for postmenopausal breast cancer and, off-label or under specific approvals, for gynecomastia and estrogen management during testosterone therapy [17]. A review of aromatase inhibitors for postmenopausal breast cancer lists fadrozole alongside exemestane, formestane, anastrozole, letrozole and vorozole as inhibitors that have been available in clinical practice, while noting toxicity as a major challenge of the class [19].

In comparison tables of aromatase inhibitors, fadrozole at 1 mg daily reduced aromatase activity by about 82 percent in postmenopausal women, and 2 mg twice daily by about 93 percent, placing it in the second generation with lower inhibition than anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane [1]. In a long-term study of 11 patients taking 2 mg twice daily for up to 973 days, estradiol suppression of 50 percent or more and estrone suppression above 80 percent from baseline were maintained, with no escape from suppression, no change in cortisol and continued suppression of aldosterone [14].

Fadrozole also affects aldosterone synthesis. A review of aldosterone synthase inhibition notes that the first orally active aldosterone synthase inhibitor, LCI699, is structurally similar to FAD286, the dextro-enantiomer of fadrozole [20]. A review of cytochrome P450 enzymes lists fadrozole among drugs whose metabolism involves CYP2A6 [21].

Fadrozole is 4-(5,6,7,8-tetrahydroimidazo[1,5-a]pyridin-5-yl)benzonitrile (C14H13N3, molar mass about 223 g/mol), used as the hydrochloride salt [1]. A 1991 Journal of Medicinal Chemistry paper described it as a potent, selective nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor [1].

Fadrozole has been used experimentally to inhibit aromatase in animals. A short-term fathead minnow reproduction assay reported a concentration-dependent reduction in fecundity with fadrozole [2]. In zebrafish, dietary fadrozole produced dose-dependent masculinization of genetic females, with 100 percent masculinized at the higher doses [3][16], and treatment of fry of the Siamese fighting fish produced mostly males with behavioral changes [15]. Brain aromatase inhibition has been used to examine neuroprotection [4][5]. Adverse outcome pathway modelling for endocrine disruptors has also drawn on fadrozole studies [6].

The T Nation forum article and discussion on estradiol lists fadrozole among Type II aromatase inhibitors, together with anastrozole and letrozole, which act by reversibly binding the enzyme and interfering with its heme iron group [18]. Fadrozole is prescription-only and not approved in most countries [1].

Human clinical work is in breast cancer. In a randomized trial of 80 previously treated postmenopausal women with metastatic breast cancer given 1 or 4 mg daily, toxicity was mild to moderate (hot flushes 28 percent, nausea and vomiting 13 percent, fatigue 8 percent, loss of appetite 5 percent), overall response was 23 percent, and there was no significant difference between doses [10][11]. A phase 2 study of 56 patients found a 14 percent response rate across three dosing schedules, with a median response duration of 36 months and mild to moderate subjective toxicity [12]. A further randomized study of 80 women after tamoxifen failure reported a 17 percent objective response rate and low incidence of side effects [13].

A meta-analysis of aromatase inhibitors in advanced breast cancer and studies of HER-2 levels and response to hormone therapy also include fadrozole [7][8][9]. No studies were found testing fadrozole for appearance, muscle or body composition.

timeline.event: Fadrozole hydrochloride described as a potent, selective nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor [1].
Randomized trials in postmenopausal women with metastatic breast cancer reported [10][11].
Long-term suppression of estrogen over up to 973 days reported in 11 patients [14].
Phase 2 and randomized studies after tamoxifen failure published [12][13].

name: Fadrozole

card.summary: A nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer in Japan and as a lab tool; nothing tested for looks.
card.note: No appearance studies; sources give little on side effects.

quick.overview:
Fadrozole (Afema) is an oral aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer in Japan. Outside oncology it mainly appears in animal and lab research as a way to block estrogen production.
No human trial has examined it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It reversibly binds the heme group of aromatase, reducing conversion of androgens to estrogens by about 80 to 90 percent at tested doses.
quick.risks: It is prescription-only and not approved in most countries.
